title: Stuart Attwell deliberately kept off Nottingham Forest matches for two years by PGMO
content:
Stuart Attwell, the Premier League referee, is being deliberately kept off Nottingham Forest matches due to his controversial history with the club.

It is two years to the day since Attwell was involved in a Forest game — a 2-0 defeat against Everton that led to the club posting an infamous tweet condemning his decision-making as the video assistant referee (VAR) and noting he was a fan of Luton Town, one of their relegation rivals at the time.

There are no indications when the Professional Game Match Officials Limited (PGMO), the organising body for referees in English football, will reintroduce Attwell to Forest matches in any capacity.

As well as not refereeing games, Attwell has been left off VAR and fourth-official duties for all the Forest matches in the relevant two-year period.

PGMO sources, speaking on condition of anonymity as they did not have permission to talk publicly, have confirmed it relates to what happened at Everton two years ago and a controversy that ended with Forest being charged by the English Football Association for an “attack on the integrity of a match official on an unparalleled scale”.

Forest’s tweet, now deleted, was posted from their official channel. “Three extremely poor decisions — three penalties not given — which we simply cannot accept,” it read. “We warned the PGMO that the VAR is a Luton fan before the game but they didn’t change him. Our patience has been tested multiple times. NFFC will now consider its options.”

In January this year, Attwell was chosen to be the fourth official for Forest’s FA Cup third-round tie at Wrexham. For unexplained reasons, he was subsequently replaced by Darren England without any announcement. PGMO has declined to clarify why.

What remains unclear is whether the decision to keep him away from Forest matches has been taken entirely by Attwell’s bosses or whether the referee himself has indicated in any way that it might not be a good idea to assign him to the club’s fixtures.

However, it appears similar to previous cases when referees involved in major flashpoints are deliberately kept away from the relevant teams.

Mark Clattenburg, then a Premier League referee, had a six-year exile from Everton’s Goodison Park after making several decisions, which he has since admitted were big mistakes, in Liverpool’s favour during a Merseyside derby in 2007. Martin Atkinson was kept off Manchester United matches after a series of issues involving Sir Alex Ferguson and the manager’s assistant, Carlos Queiroz.

In Attwell’s case, everything exploded spectacularly when he turned down three penalty appeals for Forest in a defeat that left them one point above Luton in the relegation zone.

A regulatory commission ruled that Forest’s tweet alleged possible bias on Attwell’s part and fined the club £750,000 (nearly $1million at the time), a record punishment for an offence involving social media.

The FA had been seeking a punishment of at least £1million for what it described as an “egregious, direct and public attack”. The club appealed against the “disproportionate” punishment, but without success.

Attwell, who refereed Tottenham Hotspur’s 2-2 home draw against Brighton & Hove Albion on Saturday, became the youngest referee to officiate in the Premier League, aged 25, when he was fast-tracked through the system in 2008.

However, he and one of his assistants, Nigel Bannister, were censured in his debut season after awarding the infamous ‘ghost goal’ to Reading in a game at Watford in September 2008, mistakenly believing the ball had gone into the net when it had, in fact, gone wide.

Attwell, who is on the FIFA list of international referees and has taken charge of European and international matches, was the subject of another complaint from Forest when he turned down a penalty in a key promotion fixture at Bournemouth in May 2022.

An incorrect offside decision was given instead and Steve Cooper, Forest’s head coach at the time, said after the game that Attwell and his assistant had “put their hands up and owned up to a huge error.”

By Graham Scott, former Premier League referee

How much say do clubs have over which referees are appointed to their matches?

Too much, I’d say, but the body responsible for dispatching officials to matches around the country is in a bind, whatever it does.

Over the years, some referees have been kept apart from clubs and away from their stadiums after making ‘controversial’ (aka, wrong) decisions that have cost a team points.

Clattenburg’s absence from Goodison Park for seven seasons was the most notable example, but The Athletic has revealed that Attwell has deliberately been kept away from Forest matches.

Forest are not the only team to go public with complaints and criticisms, or announce through their social media channels that they have fired off an angry missive to PGMO chief Howard Webb because one of his referees was not to their liking.

Clubs should not be allowed to choose who referees their matches, but it sometimes feels they have a de facto veto if they make enough fuss.

PGMO employs England’s top referees and announces the appointments each Monday afternoon. It keeps its responses private, but clubs seem to take comfort and joy when they receive an acknowledgement — never an apology — that an error was made.

The dilemma for PGMO is how long to leave it before appointing the same referee to that team again.

League secretaries of yesteryear would assert their authority by sending a referee back straightaway after complaints, as if to make it clear that they appoint the officials, not the clubs. I admired that approach, even if I was rather apprehensive on my return.

Nowadays, there is a more conservative approach, for fear that the referee will become the story before kick-off.

Some referees prefer to stay away from certain teams or venues, too, even if that is down to a superstitious feeling that a stadium is not a happy hunting ground.

Decisions about who goes where are ultimately signed off by Webb, and I am not aware of any referee refusing an appointment in such circumstances. But the referee does get a say in their frequent appraisals, and by and large, a sensible balance is struck.
